utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-98-32-PT, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances. Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, representing the Prosecution together with Dermot Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vladimir Domazet. I represent Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasiljevic, are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again now that you have your earphones on. Are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is a Status Conference called in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 bis. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're here. I don't know what matters Your Honours wish to be addressed on at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, there's very little that we can do because the position about when this case will be heard and by whom will not be resolved until late next month at the elections. But it seems to be proceeding with the -- we now have a pre-trial brief, but I think it would be unwise to make any further orders in relation to that at this stage. It's no good having all the parties absolutely ready and then having to wait a couple of months before the trial commences. We do have a motion from you, though, for a medical examination. Is this by consent?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have spoken to Mr. Domazet this morning. We were aware, may I say, that he didn't object, but we thought that we had better do it formally by way of written motion. I have spoken again to Mr. Domazet this morning who has very helpfully told us that he has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it has to be something more than that, I'm afraid, because, you see, we are compelling the accused to testify against himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, the Rule which we looked at -- yes, Your Honour, Rule 74 bis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "... may, at the request of a party, order a medical, psychiatric or psychological examination of the accused." I don't actually see anything in the Rule that says there has to be anything more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Rules don't overcome the Statute, though. The Statute says, in perfectly clear language, that the accused is entitled to the minimum guarantee of not being compelled to testify against himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting that it can't be done by consent. It clearly can. From the attitude that the accused, through Mr. Domazet, has previously expressed about this alibi matter, they obviously are very confident and they probably will consent. But I think it has to be by consent and not merely, "do not object." You can see that this may arise later, and I'd like to get the procedural parts of it straight.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in our submission, it would be rather like the taking of fingerprints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Precisely, and that is something which a Statute is required; indeed, a hotly-disputed legality even to some Statutes, certainly in my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, it's the same in my jurisdiction, but there are Statutes which say that fingerprints may be taken, and if there is a refusal, there can be the forced taking of fingerprints, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My point is, I think, a fairly simple one; the Appeals Chamber has said that the Rules are subject to the Statute and that the Plenary meeting of the Judges cannot enact the law through the medium of the Rules so that the Rules can only be procedural, and certainly you may make an application. But if there was an objection, I do not understand how you could possibly succeed in light of Article 21 of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know whether Your Honour wants to hear argument on this at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that we deal with it in a very much straightforward way. I'll ask Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, does your client consent to this examination? As I understand it, it's in order to demonstrate whether he was indeed the patient who was in hospital at the time shown in the medical records, and you have, as I understand it, been very cooperative in enabling all the tests necessary to ascertain the validity of those records, and this is the next step. But I take the view myself that we do need a consent from your client to such an examination, X-rays and blood tests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Personally, I've gone through these documents, and I'm sure that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic was at the hospital and he was there since the 14th of June, 1992, and I have not objected -- I did not object to all the examinations required for the reason that I have just received this morning in my locker this document, but I have not had the opportunity to speak with my client Mr. Vasiljevic about the fact. Personally, I'm not opposed to that, and I've said so to Ms. Korner this morning. However, maybe it would be better if I could have the opportunity to talk to my client and then I could tell you if we object or not to this examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But, Mr. Domazet, I want something more than a mere absence of objection. What we need is your client's consent to having these examinations. Now, certainly I think it would be very advisable for you to speak to your client, and whilst you are here today, this would be the opportunity to do so, but I don't want any documents subsequently filed merely to say that your client does not object. We want the words that he consents to it, if that be the case. If he does not, then Ms. Korner apparently has some argument which may overcome it, but I think that this will be the most direct and straightforward way of disposing of it if we can. And if Ms. Korner wants to argue that, notwithstanding the absence of such a consent, the Prosecution is still entitled to have the accused testify against himself, then we'll hear that argument, or perhaps it can be done in writing. So would you please arrange to have this conference with your client today and, if possible, file some document today so that the matter can be disposed of, hopefully without any further ado. But, otherwise, we will await what you have to say in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I agree with your proposal. I'll comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is there anything else that the Prosecution wants to raise, Ms. Korner? I don't want there to be some constitutional argument that goes up to the Appeals Chamber on a matter like this if we can avoid it. I'm not being obstructive, I hasten to add, but I am concerned that I, at least, comply with the terms of the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware from other cases that Your Honour takes the view that certain matters may be seen to be compelling a person to give evidence against themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You say that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You say that in terms which suggest that you don't believe that anybody else does, but I'll take that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to start 2001 off by disagreeing with Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it is, I think, a matter of some importance. I have been involved in a lot of litigation dealing with this sort of thing, and there are some very real problems involved in it if it has to be argued. That's all I can say. I think that in most of the cases I have argued, I ended up losing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say that I don't think from what, as Your Honour has already remarked, has been the attitude throughout of Mr. Domazet and Mr. Vasiljevic there is likely to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. That's why I would rather deal with it in that sort of a way rather than have to deal with it as a matter of some constitutional importance to the Statute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other matter, and I appreciate the problems there are about setting a date or even deciding how this case is going to be heard because of the administrative changes that may or may not happen in this building, but I don't know whether Your Honour is able to assist on this: In the light of the fact that in Your Honour's list there are two cases awaiting trial, if not a third, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is a third but it's a long way away somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's a long way down the list. Is Your Honour able to give any indication, given that this case is a great deal shorter on any showing than the other case, whether it is this case that is likely to be taken first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let me explain it to you this way: Sometime at the end of February or early in March, we will know who has and who has not been re-elected. There are a number Judges who are not standing for re-election anyway, and the President has discussed this with the Bureau in an endeavour to determine what these Judges can be put to in their remaining time. It is a very short case, this, in the sense that it will probably be over and done with in two, two and a half months, I would think, and it seems an ideal case to be given to three of the Judges who are not standing for re-election so that they can dispose of it by the end of the year. Now, it is, of all the cases which are ready or almost ready for trial, this is clearly the best case for that purpose, and I rather suspect that may happen. What is going to happen, and this is anticipated will happen, when ad hoc Judges come on stream in the middle of the year, whichever Trial Chamber has just finished a case or is just about to finish a case will be split up into two or perhaps three subChambers or divisions, with a permanent Judge and two ad hoc Judges or two permanent Judges and an ad hoc Judge. Those Judges will be then given the work that is remaining in that Trial Chamber's list and any others that are ready for hearing. I rather suspect that if we are the ones -- if Trial Chamber II is the one which is going to be split up, that Brdjanin and Talic will be taken by one of those divisions --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- and it will be dealt with in that way. If we are not the Trial Chamber that's split up, then we will be starting Brdjanin and Talic at the conclusion of the current Krnojelac case, provided that we're all re-elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You see the state of indecision we're in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's a funny position to be in, to be subject to election as Judges, I can tell you, and I have found it quite strange. Nevertheless, we are in the situation where we just cannot finalise any judicial arrangements for the rest of this year until we know. That is why the United Nations agreed to move the elections to an earlier spot than they usually are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to Your Honour. That is of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid you'll have to share the indecision with us, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, are there any matters you want to raise in terms of the Rule about the matter -- about the case, about your client's well-being, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, nothing, nothing related to the Status Conference and the issues that ought to be raised during the Status Conference. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you. If there's nothing else, we'll adjourn. The next matter starting in this courtroom starts at 10.00.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
